# Abolition of judicial torture; proportionate, certain punishment (`abolition_of_torture`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by habeas_corpus_fair_trial, utilitarianism
- Core idea: Torture to obtain confessions tests endurance, not guilt: the weak innocent confess and name others, the tough guilty go free, so every conviction it produces is worthless as evidence. Crime is deterred by the certainty and promptness of a moderate punishment far more than by the cruelty of a rare one, and public cruelty hardens the public. The argument must also offer a replacement: continental courts tortured because their law demanded a confession or two eyewitnesses for conviction, so abolition requires allowing judges to convict on a careful weighing of circumstantial evidence. Witch trials supply the proof, since tortured suspects everywhere confessed to impossible things.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking torture was lawless sadism; in Roman-canon procedure it was a regulated step that needed prior partial proof, so the law of proof must change too
  - Citing museum horrors such as the iron maiden, most of which are 19th-century fabrications
  - Calling it medieval; judicial torture peaked in the 16th–17th centuries and English common law largely did without it
  - Arguing only from mercy; magistrates respond to the argument that torture convicts the innocent and lets the guilty escape
- History: china: 167 BC – Emperor Wen of Han abolishes mutilating punishments; 7th c. Tang Code limits the amount and occasions of judicial beating; india: c. 250 BC – Ashoka’s Pillar Edict IV grants condemned prisoners three days before execution for appeals or religious observance; rome: c. 215 AD – Ulpian: evidence from torture is 'fragile and dangerous' (Digest 48.18.1.23), yet its use spreads; islamic: classical law – most jurists hold a confession under duress invalid; rulers' courts tortured nonetheless; europe: 866 Pope Nicholas I condemns confession by torture; c. 1250 torture enters continental procedure; 1631 Spee, Cautio criminalis; 1754 Prussia abolishes it; 1764 Beccaria; 1786 Tuscany abolishes torture and the death penalty
- Read:
  - Cesare Beccaria, Dei delitti e delle pene (1764)
  - John H. Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof: Europe and England in the Ancien Régime (1977)
  - Friedrich Spee, Cautio criminalis (1631)
